candidate.blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort → Nutrition and Oral Hydration: assess nutritional/hydration needs, implement special diets or fluid modifications based on diagnosis and client needs, and provide nutrition-related teaching.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — individualized nutrition and fluid education in chronic heart failure
candidate.educational_objective: Teach heart-failure nutrition as an individualized plan built around a heart-healthy dietary pattern, sodium reduction, and fluid guidance when specifically indicated rather than a universal fixed restriction for every client.

options.A: Use an overall heart-healthy eating pattern, reduce sodium according to the individualized plan, and follow any fluid limit specifically recommended by the health care team.
options.B: Use one fixed low-sodium and fluid-restriction prescription for every client with heart failure regardless of congestion, laboratory findings, comorbidities, or treatment plan.
options.C: Focus only on total calories because food quality, sodium intake, and individualized fluid guidance have little relevance to heart-failure self-care.
options.D: Increase processed and restaurant foods because they are generally lower in sodium than minimally processed foods prepared without added salt.

candidate.rationale: Current American Heart Association guidance recommends an overall heart-healthy dietary pattern that emphasizes vegetables and fruits, whole grains, healthy protein sources, unsaturated fats, minimally processed foods, and reduced sodium. Heart-failure self-care guidance also addresses sodium reduction and states that some clients may be advised to limit fluid intake, with the daily amount determined by the health care team. The AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline notes that evidence for specific universal sodium and fluid restrictions in heart failure is limited, so these measures should not be converted into one fixed prescription for every client. Therefore, A is correct. B overgeneralizes restrictions, C ignores established nutrition/self-care domains, and D reverses current sodium-reduction guidance.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Directly supports a heart-healthy dietary pattern with sodium reduction and individualized fluid guidance, while explicitly avoiding a universal fluid or sodium prescription for all heart-failure clients.
candidate.source_document_title: 2026 Dietary Guidance to Improve Cardiovascular Health; Lifestyle Changes for Heart Failure; 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure
candidate.source_locator: AHA 2026 Dietary Guidance → Top Things to Know item 7: heart-healthy pattern emphasizes vegetables/fruits, whole grains, healthy proteins, unsaturated fats, minimally processed foods, reduced added sugars and sodium. AHA 'Lifestyle Changes for Heart Failure' → 'Track your daily fluid intake': some people with HF may be advised to limit fluid and should ask the health care professional how much to drink; 'Eat for a healthy heart' describes the overall heart-healthy pattern. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline → Sections 7.1.1-7.1.2 and 8.2: HF self-care includes sodium restriction, but specific sodium thresholds and routine fluid restriction are supported by limited/low-quality evidence and should not be universalized.
candidate.source_organization: American Heart Association; American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology/Heart Failure Society of America
candidate.source_version_date: AHA dietary guidance updated 2026-03-31; HF lifestyle guidance current 2026; HF guideline 2022-04-01
